meetings.title: Maya / Daniel 1:1
segments: Hey Daniel. Morning for you, right? How's it going?
Morning, yes. Good. The Zendesk backfill shipped yesterday, so now new workspaces can import ninety days of history.
It's hidden in settings for now, but it works.
How long does the backfill take for a big account?
For ninety days of a large Zendesk account, maybe forty thousand tickets, about twenty minutes.
We rate limit ourselves so we don't hit their API limits.
The user sees a progress bar and gets an email when it's done.
That's fast enough to put in onboarding.
Nobody minds waiting twenty minutes if they know it's working.
That's great. We should think about where that lives in onboarding.
Agreed. The other thing is the SSO versus Jira one-pager.
I have a draft, and I'd love your eyes on it before the alignment meeting.
How long is it right now?
Three pages, which I know isn't really a one-pager.
It has the request data, the revenue at stake, effort estimates, and a section on risks.
I wanted to be thorough, because I know people will challenge it.
Being thorough is good, but put the thoroughness in an appendix.
The first page should be readable in two minutes.
Most people in the meeting will only read that page.
Sure. What's your recommendation?
SSO first. But honestly I'm nervous about it.
Tom's team has been asking about Jira for months, and I feel like I'm about to tell them no again.
What's the actual conversation you're dreading with Tom?
That his team has been promising customers Jira for a while, based on things we said six months ago.
So when it moves again, it's his team's credibility on the line, not mine.
That's a real problem, and it's partly on me for saying 'soon' six months ago.
The fix is a real date.
If we commit to Q1 and hit it, Tom's team gets their credibility back.
I get that. A couple of things.
First, I read the draft this morning.
It's good, but it buries the recommendation on page two.
Lead with it. And add Aisha's pipeline numbers, because the revenue case is what makes SSO obvious.
That makes sense. I'll get the pipeline numbers from Aisha and revise the one-pager.
Second, on Tom. Don't let him hear it for the first time in the meeting.
I'll give him a preview beforehand.
And think about whether there's a small Jira thing you can offer, so it's not just 'no.'
What will you tell Tom, exactly?
The truth. That the revenue case for SSO is overwhelming this quarter, that Jira is coming in Q1 with a real date, and that we're offering a small one-way button in the meantime.
And I'll ask for his help with the customers who've been waiting.
That's much better than him hearing it cold in the meeting. Thank you.
That's what previews are for.
Nobody likes surprises in a big meeting.
Actually, yes. A lot of the Jira requests are really just 'let me create an issue from this.'
A one-way button would cover most of them, and it's small.
What would the button actually do? Walk me through it.
From any theme, you click 'create Jira issue'.
It opens a small form with the title pre-filled from the theme label, the description filled with the summary and the top three quotes, and a link back to the theme.
You pick the project, and that's it. No syncing back.
That's genuinely useful. I'd use that myself.
Should the button be available to everyone, or only admins?
Everyone who can see the theme.
The whole point is to lower the friction between spotting a problem and getting it to the team that can fix it.
If admins have to do it, it'll pile up.
Makes sense. I'll put that in the recommendation.
Put that in the one-pager as part of the recommendation.
Anything you want from me?
Feedback on how I'm managing?
One thing. I don't always know how you're weighing things when we prioritize.
Revenue, retention, strategy. If I knew the criteria, I could bring you better recommendations, instead of guessing.
What would you want the criteria to look like?
Even something simple. Like, revenue at risk or blocked, number of customers affected, strategic fit, and effort.
With rough weights. Then when I recommend something, I can show the scoring and we argue about the inputs, not the conclusion.
I like that. Arguing about inputs is much healthier.
Is there anything else? Something that would make your week easier?
Fewer interrupt requests from sales for one-off integrations.
Every week someone asks if we can connect to some tool for one prospect.
I want to help, but it fragments my time.
Let's route those through Aisha's weekly roadmap sync instead of direct messages.
Then they get prioritized with everything else, and you're not the bottleneck.
That would help a lot.
I'll tell the sales team.
That's a very good point.
I'll write down the prioritization criteria I actually use and share them with the PM team.
It'll help everyone, not just you.
When do you think you'd have the criteria written down?
End of next week. I'll draft it, share it with you and the other PMs for comments, and then we'll use it in the next planning cycle.
Great. I'm happy to be a guinea pig for it with the SSO work.
Deal. You'll be the first test case.
Thank you. And on growth, I'd really like to own SSO end to end.
Requirements, rollout, the enterprise admin area, all of it.
I think you should. If the alignment meeting goes the way I expect, SSO is yours.
Treat it as the start of an enterprise platform area you lead, not a one-off project.
What would you need to see from me to make that a formal role?
Ship SSO on the date we commit to, run the security review well, and build a relationship with two or three enterprise customers' IT teams.
If that happens, I'll make the case for a lead PM title next cycle.
And ask me for help early if anything slips.
Surprises are the only thing I really mind.
That's clear. Thank you, Maya.
That's exactly what I was hoping to hear.
